Capsular contracture

In the 42-person blinded trial, PBM did not outperform placebo on patient-reported symptoms or most clinical ratings, while the placebo group improved more on softness and contracture grade. A prior uncontrolled series reported improvement but does not establish a treatment effect.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In the 42-person blinded trial, PBM did not outperform placebo on patient-reported symptoms or most clinical ratings, while the placebo group improved more on softness and contracture grade. A prior uncontrolled series reported improvement but does not establish a treatment effect.

Summary of the Evidence

Two independent human publications studied low-level laser treatment for established breast-implant capsular contracture. One was a 33-patient single-arm series and the other a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial with 42 participants. The controlled trial followed patients for six months. No animal or cell-culture study specific to this indication was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

The 33-person uncontrolled series reported that 93.9% avoided surgery and that patients experienced less breast stiffness and improved comfort after treatment. Without a control group, the report cannot determine whether improvement was caused by PBM, natural symptom fluctuation, expectation, or other care (Johnson et al. 2015).

The more informative randomized trial found no significant difference between PBM and placebo in patient-reported symptoms or clinician assessments of breast symmetry, shape, and naturalness. At both one and six months, the placebo group had greater improvement in clinician-rated softness and degree of contracture. Thus, the controlled comparison did not confirm the earlier series' favorable impression (Azimi et al. 2018).

Animal evidence

No animal study of PBM for breast-implant capsular contracture was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Both reports used 904-nm near-infrared laser treatment. The single-arm series reported 1.5 J/cm², 600 seconds per session, and six sessions. The randomized trial used six weekly sessions over six weeks, but the database does not report its delivered fluence or irradiance. The series' dosimetry should not be assumed to describe the randomized trial simply because both used 904-nm light. No comparison of doses or treatment schedules was performed.

Interpretation

The controlled trial found no added benefit over placebo on patient symptoms or most clinical measures, and placebo improved more on two clinician-rated outcomes. The uncontrolled series reported improvement, but its design cannot resolve the contrast. Current evidence does not establish PBM as an effective treatment for capsular contracture.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)Low for clinical benefit over placebo in established capsular contracture

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The double-blind trial of 42 patients found no advantage over placebo for symptoms, breast shape, or most clinician ratings, while placebo improved more on softness and contracture grade. A prior 33-person uncontrolled series reported improvement but cannot identify treatment effects. A larger sham-controlled study with standardized grading, patient symptoms, and reoperation follow-up would clarify the result.
